quiz.question: What share of one-year-old children in the world have been vaccinated against at least one disease?

headline: Nearly Nine Out of Ten Toddlers Got the Jab — and the World Barely Noticed
teaser: Somewhere in the background of the past four decades, a health revolution has been unfolding with the kind of determined unglamour that guarantees it will never trend on social media. It involves cold chains across deserts, motorbikes on unpaved roads, and an army of community health workers whose names you will never learn. The question is simple: what share of the world's babies have been reached? Most people, including those who think of themselves as reasonably informed about global health, guess a number that would have been roughly correct in the mid-1980s. The world, as it has an annoying habit of doing, moved on without updating anyone's assumptions.
metaDescription: About 86% of the world's one-year-olds have received at least one vaccine dose, up from 20% in 1980. 72% of people dramatically underestimate this.
summary: In 1980, only about one in five of the world's infants received even a single vaccine dose. Today, that figure stands at roughly 86%. This is one of the most sweeping public-health achievements in human history — a fourfold increase in coverage across every continent, delivered to villages with no paved roads and cities with no reliable electricity. It happened so gradually that almost nobody registered it as news, which is, if you think about it, rather the point of good public health.
nuance: The global average conceals stubborn pockets of under-vaccination. About 14 million children still receive zero routine vaccine doses each year — so-called 'zero-dose' children — concentrated in conflict zones and remote rural areas. COVID-19 disrupted immunisation campaigns in 2020-2021, causing a temporary dip, and recovery has been uneven. Vaccine hesitancy in high-income countries, meanwhile, threatens coverage from the other direction.
aside: Consider the logistics: delivering temperature-sensitive vials to 130 million newborns a year, across deserts, mountains, and monsoon seasons, in countries where the postal service sometimes cannot deliver a letter. And yet it works. One begins to suspect that humans are considerably better at organising things when nobody is trying to take credit.

emailDigestLine: From one in five to nearly nine in ten — the quiet triumph of the cold chain and the community health worker.
premiumTeaser: The story of how vaccination went from a rich-country luxury to a near-universal norm involves a retired Rotarian, a surprisingly effective donkey-based delivery network, and the single most cost-effective health intervention ever measured. The premium deep-dive follows the cold chain from factory floor to a health post in rural Chad.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Ask students to guess the 1980 figure before revealing. Connects to SDG 3 (Good Health) and provides a case study in global logistics, cold-chain infrastructure, and the economics of public goods.
publishingNote: WUENIC and OWID data are closely aligned. Nuance addresses zero-dose children and COVID disruption honestly.

learn.title: "Every Last Child" documentary (UNICEF)
learn.description: Follows the cold chain from factory floor to remote health post — the logistics behind the 20% to 86% climb on this chart. It makes the motorbikes-on-unpaved-roads reality tangible.

fund.description: UNICEF procures and delivers vaccines to over 100 countries. The 86% coverage figure on this chart is, in large part, UNICEF's supply chain made visible in data.
fund.impact: $2 = enough vaccine doses to protect one child against polio

act.action: Check your own vaccination records are up to date
act.description: The 86% figure on this chart tracks children — but adult boosters lapse quietly. Checking your own records takes ten minutes and closes a gap that most people do not realise they have.
